title: Rockaway Traditional Land
summary: Rockaway and Reckouwacky names belong to a coastal world of villages, bays, islands, travel routes, diplomacy, and land records across western Long Island and present-day Brooklyn/Queens. The territory is remembered alongside neighboring Merrick and Canarsie landscapes, not as an isolated place.
why_this_matters: Rockaway Traditional Land presents western Long Island, Jamaica Bay, Hempstead Bay, and the south shore islands as Native homeland. It connects early records with waterways, coastal movement, and the continued importance of public memory.
history_content:
Early colonial sources describe Rockaway villages, south shore waterways, and involvement in Hempstead-area land records. Rockaway history overlaps with Merrick, Massapequa, Canarsie, and other western Long Island communities through diplomacy, trade, kinship, and colonial pressure.

Named-source moments include the 1639 western Long Island deed boundary reaching from Rockaway, the 1643 Hempstead deed context linking Rockaway with Massapequa and Merrick-related communities, the 1655 Rockaway Neck deed naming Ruckquaheag, Ronnessoke/Suscaneman, Adam/Achitteronose, and others, and the 1657 Hempstead conference naming Mangwobe of Rockaway with Tackapousha, Wyandanch, Cockenoe, and Merrick representatives. [1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911).; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV.]

Village and archaeological references are kept broad so sensitive places are not mapped for visitation.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The illustrated southeast wedge between Canarsie and Merrick, focused on eastern Jamaica Bay, southern Queens, and the Rockaway Peninsula without extending into western Jamaica Bay land assigned to Canarsie in the reference-guided display. The transition toward Merrick and Canarsie is generalized across modern shoreline land pieces.
